Air strikes hit warehouses and factory in Yemen’s Sanaa, Houthi authorities say
A series of heavy air strikes hit Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, with Houthi authorities reporting damage to a food storage warehouse, a warehouse and a factory belonging to the Yemeni-Saudi Mineral Water Company, Al Jazeera reported.
The attacks followed claims by the Houthis’ military spokesman that the group had carried out four operations deep inside Saudi Arabia, targeting King Khalid airport, a financial centre and a petrochemicals company in Riyadh, as well as Khamis Mushait airbase.
The spokesperson said the attacks were in retaliation for an air strike on a boat carrying displaced people at the port of Ras al-Ara in southern Yemen.
He said 19 of the 25 people aboard were killed and four were wounded, with their bodies scattered along the coast.

MP calls for pre-emptive strike on US warships
An Iranian MP has called for a pre-emptive strike on US aircraft carriers deployed east of the Strait of Hormuz, describing an attack as essential to breaking the current “neither war nor peace” deadlock between Tehran and Washington.
Amir Hayat-Moqaddam, a member of parliament's National Security Commission, told the 7 Sobh daily that “a pre-emptive attack on American warships is an absolute necessity”.
He said Iran should strike vessels stationed 700 to 800km east of the strait, “damage them and drive them out of the region”.
Hayat-Moqaddam is one of several Iranian officials to have called for pre-emptive attacks, as debate continues over how Tehran should respond to the threat of renewed US-Israel military attacks.
These officials argue that demonstrating Iran's military strength is necessary to deter another US attack.
Washington, Hayat-Moqaddam said, must understand that it would suffer greater losses in any renewed conflict, adding Iran "should already have carried out such attacks".
He also dismissed the prospect of productive negotiations with Washington, saying talks were necessary mainly to convince domestic and international public opinion that Tehran was not seeking war.
“Negotiations with America are fruitless,” he said, pointing to two occasions when Iran was attacked during negotiations.

data.author: Mee User
data.summary:
India's Rahul Gandhi backs continued arms trade with Israel despite Gaza genocide
India's opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has defended continued military cooperation with Israel, saying New Delhi should maintain strong strategic ties with the country despite international outrage over the war on Gaza.
The leader of the Indian National Congress made the remarks during a discussion with political scientist Robert Pape at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, where he spoke about India's position in global affairs.
"We have good relations with Israel, and we buy weapons from them," Gandhi said. "I fully support maintaining good relations with Israel."
He argued that India had strategic reasons to maintain military ties with Israel, and said New Delhi should be free to procure the weapons it considers best for its armed forces rather than allow its foreign policy to be dictated by the priorities of other countries.
Gandhi briefly condemned Israel's actions in Gaza, but slammed the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, saying the killing of civilians was unacceptable.
"But we are a much bigger country, with a population of 1.5 billion, and our foreign policy should be based on what is good for us, not on what is good for others," he added.

data.author: Mee User

Israeli forces detain recently released prisoners in West Bank raids
Israeli forces have raided homes and arrested several Palestinians, including recently released prisoners, across the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.
At dawn, soldiers arrested Muadh Nader Sawafta, 23, in the village of Tubas, and Naji Ibrahim Bisharat, 50, in the nearby town of Tammun, south of Tubas.
Kamal Bani Odeh, director of the Palestinian Prisoners Society in Tubas, said that Sawafta had been released from Israeli detention two months ago.
Israeli forces had detained 20 young men from the two villages the previous night, most of them from Tubas, before releasing them, the report said.
In a separate raid on Friday, Israeli forces arrested three Palestinians in Qarawa Bani Hassan, southwest of Nablus. One of them was a former prisoner who had been released just two days earlier after spending two years in Israeli prisons, according to Wafa.
Earlier on Friday, soldiers raided homes in the Iktaba neighbourhood, east of Tulkarem, and arrested three Palestinians. Local sources identified one of them as Jihad al-Qazli, a former prisoner from Nur Shams refugee camp.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Sudan war fuels an invisible economy of survival
data.author: Osama Abuzaid
data.summary:
Sudan war fuels an invisible economy of survival
Submitted by
Osama Abuzaid
on
Wed, 11/18/2026 - 15:42
Banks are closed, supply chains have snapped, and the state has little left to offer. From this vacuum, an alternative system has emerged
Charity workers prepare food at a shelter kitchen in Sudan’s eastern city of Gedaref, on 20 August 2024 (Ebrahim Hamid/AFP)
Off
On a Friday night in the UK city of Leeds, a nurse taps “send”. Thousands of miles away, a phone buzzes in a courtyard in Omdurman, Sudan, and a ledger of trust begins to turn.
She does not think of this as economics. She thinks of it as family obligation - not as finance, and certainly not as policy. Yet the journey of that single payment, from a British bank account to a pot of lentils shared among displaced neighbours, is a map of how Sudan survives.
It is a journey across a collapsing currency. Before the war, a dollar bought roughly 600 Sudanese pounds. Last month it passed 10,000, and the currency is still sliding.
Shopkeepers have shuttered their stores rather than sell at a loss when the rate lurches overnight. Average incomes have fallen to levels last seen in 1992, while government revenues dropped from roughly 10 percent of GDP in 2022 to below five in 2024.
Banks are closed across conflict zones, supply chains have snapped, and the state has little left to offer. In this vacuum, ordinary Sudanese have built something else.
The mechanics are unforgiving. Sudan imports most of its wheat, so every fall in the pound affects the price of bread; bakeries in Khartoum have closed as wheat and fuel costs climb. The country’s finance minister attributes the slide to demand for dollars as imports outstrip exports.
For a household, that abstraction becomes simple: the money earned this morning buys less by evening.

Thursday's landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), holding Myanmar responsible for genocide against its Rohingya minority, has raised alarm among Israeli officials and legal experts over its potential implications for the genocide case against Israel over Gaza.
"This is a dangerous precedent," a senior Israeli official told Ynet, referring to the ruling, which marked the first time the ICJ had found a state responsible for committing genocide.
"This sets parameters and standards that, admittedly, you can't apply one-to-one to Israel, but it opens the door," the official added. While Israel's case in Gaza is "more complicated", the ruling "certainly doesn't do us any good".
Another Israeli official told the public broadcaster Kan 11 that the decision reflected "worrying trends" at the top UN court, but insisted Israel could avoid a similar ruling in the case brought by South Africa in December 2023.
The official said Israel could withstand "any legal test", insisting that "we did not commit a genocide". They estimated that a final judgment in the Gaza genocide case would not be delivered before 2030.
Since October 2023, when Israel launched its military onslaught on the Gaza Strip following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October, UN officials, genocide experts and humanitarian organisations have accused Israel of committing genocide in the besieged enclave.

Nusseibeh visited just over two weeks ago after Duncan Smith spoke out in parliament about the UAE’s “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in Sudan” and called on the British government to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.
The former government minister told MEE that in his meeting with Nusseibeh he reiterated the position he had taken in parliament about the UAE’s involvement in Sudan - denied by Abu Dhabi - and called for the release of “two British citizens wrongly held in Dubai: Ryan Cornelius and Charles Ridley”.
Duncan Smith told Nusseibeh that the UAE needed to “cease and desist” from its involvement in the Sudan war, where Abu Dhabi has sponsored the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force found to have committed genocide in Darfur by the UN and US.
He told Nusseibeh that her UN candidacy gave the UAE a chance to do the right thing and withdraw from the war in Sudan and release Cornelius and Ridley, two British citizens who have been detained in Dubai for almost 20 years.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iraqi forces deploy to oil pipeline in Kataib Hezbollah stronghold
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Iraqi forces deploy to oil pipeline in Kataib Hezbollah stronghold
Iraq's Energy Police have begun establishing checkpoints along a major oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad, as government forces return to an area long controlled by the Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah group.
Staff Lieutenant General Hamed al-Husseini, commander of the Energy Police, told the Iraqi News Agency (INA) that officers would position checkpoints no more than 500 metres apart “to prevent smuggling and ensure their protection”.
The deployment will cover a five-kilometre stretch of the 441km (274-mile) pipeline supplying Baghdad's Dora refinery. Al-Husseini described the section as passing through “rugged, agricultural terrain”.
“The Energy Police will not allow smuggling or any tampering with the oil pipelines,” he said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Irish police raid Palestine donor Fergie Chambers’ Dublin home at behest of Trump
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Irish police raid Palestine donor Fergie Chambers’ Dublin home at behest of Trump
Irish police have raided the Dublin home of pro-Palestine donor Fergie Chambers and seized his property after a request by the Trump administration, the Irish Times reports.
Chambers, an American left-wing philanthropist, is currently facing extradition to the US from Spain, where he is detained pending a decision by a Spanish court.
If extradited and convicted on the lead charge of international money laundering, Chambers could face a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.
On Wednesday, Chambers’ partner Stella Schnabel received a call from Irish police officers from Special Branch informing her that they had forced entry into her Dublin home - seizing electronic devices and clothing - after a request from the US authorities.
They advised that she would need to arrange repairs for the doors they had smashed to gain access.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Armed men open fire on cargo ship off Yemen's coast
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Armed men open fire on cargo ship off Yemen's coast
Armed men aboard a small boat have fired at a bulk carrier about 95 nautical miles (176km) southwest of Yemen's port city of Mukalla, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The agency says the vessel's security personnel fired warning shots in response, prompting the attackers to retreat.
The ship sustained no damage, and the crew reported no injuries. The vessel has continued its journey.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli shelling wounds five Palestinians in central Gaza
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Israeli shelling wounds five Palestinians in central Gaza
Five Palestinians have been wounded, some critically, after Israeli artillery targeted an area near the al-Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza, the Wafa news agency reports.
The Palestinian news agency also says Israeli forces detonated explosives to destroy buildings east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
